title: The cards of power
subtitle: In which the thrones settle the visit, Hormuz is refused, Lavrov and Wadephul shake hands, and Paris fills the square.
lede: The cards lie on the table. No one picks them up.

yesterday.title: Tea under glass, seven days and a half-empty hall
yesterday.teaser: The ceremony is over. The deadlines remain.

body:
The chronicler opens the book on the twenty-seventh of September, a Sunday. Yesterday the seven-day plan still lay on the table, the visit of the two thrones had just ended, the white guest stood in Notre-Dame. Today the cards are turned. What was still a deadline on Friday is already an answer on Saturday.

I. The thrones settle accounts

In Washington the state visit was finished. Xi Jinping and Donald Trump had practised the gesture for three days: handshake, state dinner, a walk through the National Archives, where the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence lie under glass. Then the statements. Both sides spoke of a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity. Beijing counted eight points: reciprocal tariff cuts of thirty billion dollars on non-sensitive goods, a board of trade, the extension of earlier consultation results and — in a time when machines think faster than diplomats — a dialogue on artificial intelligence and a channel for AI incidents. Next round in November. Further meetings: APEC in Shenzhen, the G20 in Miami. The pandas for Atlanta were mentioned. The great questions — Taiwan, rare earths, deeper technology restrictions — remained unresolved. The pomp was large, the progress modest. The two thrones had drawn near without crossing blades. 1 2

II. The hall offers a hand

In the thinning hall of the United Nations something happened that had not happened in four years. Johann Wadephul and Sergey Lavrov sat at the same table. The talk lasted barely twenty minutes. Wadephul warned against the dangerous path of escalation toward Germany, Europe and NATO, recalled Leipzig and asked for grain routes across the Black Sea. Lavrov listened and later said he had heard nothing new; one could have read him the statement over the telephone. A handshake ended the encounter. The hall stayed bright; the cold stayed. 3

In the same place China’s vice-president, Han Zheng, urged that the postwar order be safeguarded. The world organisation did what it does best: it offered the room in which the contradictions become visible. The walkout on Netanyahu the day before still echoed in the corridors. 4

III. Seven days, refused

Over the burning water came the answer that yesterday was still pending. Trump said outside the White House that he had rejected the Iranian proposal. Araghchi had offered seven days: lift the naval blockade, ease the oil sanctions, release frozen funds, observe a regional ceasefire including Lebanon; then open the strait, then resume nuclear talks. The plan resembled the June memorandum. Trump stayed with no. The Iranians wanted the strait opened because they were doing so badly. He remained willing to talk, but not on these terms. Araghchi let it be known that Tehran was waiting for the official reply of the mediators. Meanwhile Saudi air defences kept intercepting Houthi drones and missiles. The water burned; the tankers waited. 5 6

IV. The eastern field

In the eastern field the blows continued. Russian and Ukrainian strikes again cost lives. Trump publicly told Zelenskyy to settle with Putin. In the corridors of the United Nations there was talk of grain and ceasefire; the lines stayed stiff. Russia showed confidence on the battlefield; Ukraine held to its demands. The thread remained open, heavy and unresolved. 7

V. The square that fills

And the white guest. In Paris hundreds of thousands filled the Champs-Élysées and the Place de la Concorde. Estimates ran between seven and eight hundred thousand people. Pope Leo XIV rode the historic avenue in the open popemobile. Mass was said on the square that once belonged to the Revolution and now belongs to the Republic. He spoke of the thirst in the human heart for God, for truth, for unity and peace. He warned that artificial intelligence must serve the human being and not become an instrument of rule. The crowd sang. In a country that guards its separation of church and state with care, the square was full. The pope travelled on to Lourdes. 8

The chronicler’s finding

So Sunday writes Saturday onward. The thrones have settled accounts without settling the quarrel. The hall has offered a hand without lifting the cold. The water has been given a deadline and a refusal. The field in the east still bleeds. The white guest has blessed the crowd and warned against the machines.

The chronicler leaves the threads open: whether Tehran, after the refusal, lays down a new sentence; whether the AI channel of the two thrones is more than a heading; whether Wadephul and Lavrov will speak again; whether Lourdes will give the pope different words from Paris. 9

Tomorrow he will read on.
